messages.author: fd48785a8ad1b6b6
messages.subject: Initialization error with exp_mod_normal()
parts:
Hi,

I'm experimenting with a hierarchical model which includes a Exponentially Modified Normal Distribution and I want to implement a parameter estimation on µ (and later extending this maybe on sigma and lambda). 
The problem is that I have initialization errors, if the loop over the sampling statement for the exp_mod_normal is longer than 54 (variable "number" in the stan-code) - and I can't explain this. If the loop is 54 or less everything works fine and I get the print output with changing values. The number 54 has no relationship with the data. The error:

[298] "Rejecting initial value:"                                                                             
[299] "  Log probability evaluates to log(0), i.e. negative infinity."                                       
[300] "  Stan can't start sampling from this initial value."                                                 
[301] "Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts. "  
[302] " Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."

All parameters are initialized by stan and I use Rstan 2.10.1 on Ubuntu 16.04. I wrote example data ranges in the comments.

What could cause this error? I already tried to initialize by myself every parameter - same error. Reducing the ranges of constrained values is difficult, because I don't have fully constrained parameters. Is the local parameter mu a problem? I read it earlier in a different discussion - but why is everything working fine for the first 54 loops? Or maybe it has really nothing to do with the loop count?

Many thanks for the help!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialization error with exp_mod_normal()
parts:
Presumably there's something wrong with the 55th entry
that leads to a zero density (or exception). Is there
anything being printed out? If you're using RStan, you
should run just a single chain without parallelization to
see the output (at least I think that's what you need
to do---I'm not an RStan expert).

It's definitely not the number of loop iterations.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Initialization error with exp_mod_normal()
parts:
Thanks for the fast answer! I already ran it with 1 unparallelized chain. So I tested a few things:

These rejection occurs on more or less large negative values for obs[k]:

    obs[k] ~ exp_mod_normal(mu[k],sigma[species[k]],lambda[species[k]]);

Like "-311.58" or "-190". A negative value like "-135.18" works fine. Then I ran a smaller model, took the output of the fit to initialize the parameters for the next model run. If I set all large negative values (the minimum is -358.2834) to a minimum of -100 and use the obtained initial values, then it starts sampling for every observation obs[k]. 

So the negative values are too large for the log-posterior? The problem is that I can't and shouldn't just adjust these values. The most negative values are near to zero. I attachted the distribution of obs. Should I use a different approach to account for this dispersal of values?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Initialization error with exp_mod_normal()
parts:
My guess is that the erfc evaluation is underflowing to 0,
and hence the entire exp_mod_normal density is underflowing to 0
and hence the total density to 0, which causes HMC to reject.
The problem we have with HMC is that we also need derivatives,
so even if the log erfc(x) might not underflow, it's derivative
will be 1 / erfc() d/dx erfc(x) and that will be prone to instability
because the erfc is not on the log scale.

It may be possible to make exp_mod_normal more stable with something
like a Taylor series expansion, but we don't really have the
resources to concentrate on that.

We're always happy to take pull requests for more stable
arithmetic functions!

I don't know if you cold scale the values in the model somehow.
If not, you'll either need a different sampler or to change the
model.

- Bob
